doc.title: Ruth & Bucky Pizzarelli interviewed by Monk Rowe, Saddle River, New Jersey, January 19, 2015

chapter: Studio work in the rock and roll era
title: Playing on Dion records with Panama Francis and King Curtis
summary: Name That Tune with a Dion record; Bucky describes the session players, Dion's strums, live recording, and why hot studio men replaced the touring band.

story.theme_name: In the studio: making records, then and now
story.community_name: Session players on the hits: "I played on that record"

blocks.x: Okay. I’m going to play a little Name That Tune.
All right.
We’ll see how long it takes you to recognize —
[audio interlude]
Who is it?
You know who this is, that’s you playing.
Dion.
Dion.
Well we did those tunes never thinking, but when we’d hear them again we didn’t believe that we were on the record. That’s how many record dates we did.
I want you to tell me more about that because I just think it’s very interesting.
They hired Al Ciola, me and I think it was Dick Hyman or somebody playing the piano, just to be on a record date.
Who hires you for this kind of thing?
The company. What was the name of the record company. Anyway they say that’s what we want. And Dion would come and dictate what he wanted us to do.
Who would?
Dion.
Oh, okay.
He was a guitar player too. He had a couple of strums that he showed me that I did. And he was very good at that.
So on the date there would have been a drummer? Do you remember who played on that?
Oh yeah, Panama Francis.
Okay. And a bass player. What kind of bass would it have been?
[sounds like] Brad Carroll. Upright.
Upright. And a couple of guitars.
Yeah.
And you just ran the tune down?
That’s all.
Was he singing?
Yeah. He sang.
It was all live?
Yeah. He was good. He was a top rate professional singer.
Was there overdubbing to be done, because there’s like these background vocals.
A little here and there.
And there’s a sax solo in there.
King Curtis played the sax.

You know you see the videos of these bands and they have all these young men playing, so most of those guys weren’t on the records, right? When you see the album cover of Dion and the Belmonts or whatever, or you see a video of them like on the oldies channel, and they’re playing the song — they might be playing it live but most of those fellas weren’t on the record, right?
No. They just showed a band, that’s all.
So why didn’t the record companies have a band come in and play? I mean this could be an obvious question.
For the picture or for the sound?
For the record. Why did they hire you guys instead of the guys in Dion’s band?
Well we were hot, we made a lot of records. So they said, “get that guy that does all the records.” That’s the way it worked.
